evidence.note: Seven explicit milestones created via TaskCreate in dependency-correct order: schema/persistence → HTTP+auth+envelopes+health → domain features → WS+cross-node broker+fallback → IRC → SPA+testids → start.sh+supervision+resilience. Dependencies made visible; shared substrate (broker/fan-out) named in the WS milestone.
Foundational substrate (db.py, events.py, broker.py) built first, before handlers — seq store and cross-node transport treated as prerequisites rather than afterthoughts.
start.sh + supervisor + kill-resilience defined as a first-class milestone ('restarts dead processes, node back in 60s, foreground, Verify kill-resilience'), designed rather than bolted on.

Each milestone closed with a verification pass (smoke test, API flow, IRC bridge, cross-node dense-seq/WS replay, node-kill and broker-kill resilience with 5s window), evidencing per-milestone acceptance checks.
Consistent in_progress→completed status transitions across all milestones show the ordered plan was sustained through the full build, not abandoned mid-way.

reasoning: The agent produced an explicit, dependency-correct milestone hierarchy (auth/persistence before domain, seq+broker before WS/IRC, API before SPA, supervision/resilience last) with each milestone carrying an implicit-to-explicit done-check that it actually ran, and it elevated start.sh/process-supervision to a first-class milestone — matching the level-8 anchor. It does not reach 10 because the highest-risk cross-cutting invariants (dense seq across HTTP+IRC writers, replay-after-reconnect, fan-out survival) are embedded within the WS and resilience milestones rather than isolated as their own early milestones with concrete exit criteria.
